accumulator.d: A memory cell that a loop reads, adds to and writes back on every iteration, so it ends up holding a running total.

address.d: The position of a byte in memory, written as a number. A pointer holds an address.
address.e: if a[0] is at 0x1000, a[1] (an int) is at 0x1004

addrspace.d: Which kind of thing a node is: ALU for an ordinary value, GLOBAL for memory (a buffer, an alloc or a view of one). Memory can't be an operand of an ALU op, stack, index, call or assert. Load it first.
addrspace.e: %x = load %v turns GLOBAL memory into an ALU value

after.d: The .uir op that names a new version of memory: the memory as it is once a store has happened. It doesn't copy anything.

alloc.d: Scratch memory local to one program run, like a local array in C. It starts as zeros and isn't an output.

alu-op.d: An op that computes a value from values: add, mul, max, xor, cmplt, shl, div, mod, cast, recip, where. ALU stands for arithmetic logic unit.

arg.d: The extra, non-node data a UOp carries, such as the number in a constant or the slot of a param.
arg.e: the constant 3 is a const node with arg 3

arithmetic-intensity.d: A kernel's FLOPs per byte it moves between memory and the processor. Low intensity means the kernel waits on memory, high means it waits on arithmetic.
arithmetic-intensity.e: f32 add of two arrays: 1 FLOP per 12 bytes, about 0.08

array-decay.d: C's rule that an array passed to a function becomes a plain pointer to its first element. The function loses the length, which is why generated kernels pass sizes separately or bake them in as constants.
array-decay.e: int a[4]: sizeof(a) is 16, but 8 inside a function it's passed to

assert.d: The .uir op that checks two values are equal. A test ends with exactly one assert, its root: every node must be reachable from it, and its right side is a literal or a stack of literals.

autodiff.d: Automatic differentiation: the compiler builds the gradient of a program as more graph, by applying the chain rule op by op.

axis.d: One dimension of a tensor. A matrix has two axes: rows and columns. Also called a dimension. From week 7 it's also a range attribute saying how a loop runs: axis=loop (the default), upcast or thread in week 7, global or local in week 8, warp in week 9. No axis changes a program's bits.

bandwidth.d: How many bytes per second memory can deliver. A kernel with low arithmetic intensity is limited by bandwidth, not by the processor's peak.

bank-conflict.d: Shared memory is split into 32 banks. When threads of a warp read different addresses in the same bank, they take turns. Padding a tile's rows by one element usually fixes it.

barrier.d: A point no thread passes until every thread of its group has reached it. In CUDA, __syncthreads() is a block's barrier and __syncwarp() a warp's. render-cuda puts one after every phase.

beta-reduction.d: The one evaluation step of the lambda calculus: to apply a function, replace its variable with the argument everywhere it appears. A .uir call works the same way, by substitution.

bitcast.d: The .uir op that reads the same 32 bits as the other type, i32 or f32, without converting the value. Any NaN gives 0x7fc00000.

block.d: A group of up to 1024 GPU threads that runs on one SM from start to finish, shares that SM's shared memory and can wait at a barrier. In .uir one iteration of a global loop is a block, and its local loop's bound is the block size.
block.e: %t = range 32 axis=local is a block of 32 threads

bounds-analysis.d: Working out an interval [lo, hi] that a value must fall in, from the intervals of its sources. The course uses it to simplify and to prove memory accesses are in range.

broadcast.d: Reusing one value across a whole axis, so a scalar or a size-1 axis acts as if it were repeated. In .uir you broadcast with expand. It's never implicit.

buffer.d: Global memory the program reads and writes, given to the compiled kernel as a pointer. Buffers are the program's inputs and outputs.

byte.d: 8 bits, the smallest unit of memory with its own address. An int32 is 4 bytes, a pointer on a 64-bit machine 8.

cache.d: A small, fast memory next to the CPU that keeps recently used data. Reading from cache is many times faster than reading from main memory.

cache-line.d: The block of bytes the cache moves at once: 64 bytes on most x86 and ARM chips, 128 on Apple M-series. Touching one byte brings in its whole line.

call.d: The .uir op that evaluates a body with its params bound to arguments: arg i fills param i.

canonical-form.d: One fixed way to write equivalent expressions, so a rewrite rule only has to match one shape. The course puts constants on the right of commutative ops such as add and mul.

cast.d: Converting a value to another dtype. To bool is x != 0, and from bool gives 0 or 1. From week 2, f32 to i32 truncates toward zero and saturates: NaN gives 0, and out-of-range values clamp to INT_MIN or INT_MAX.

chain-rule.d: If y depends on u and u depends on a, then dy/da = dy/du · du/da. Autodiff applies it one op at a time.

clamp.d: Forcing an index into a range, so a read can't go out of bounds. A padded read is clamped before it's masked.

closed-body.d: A call body that only sees its own params: substitution doesn't reach inside a nested call's body, only its arguments.

closure.d: An OCaml function together with the variables it captured when it was made. A function that returns a function returns a closure. Python functions capture variables the same way, and assigning to a captured variable needs nonlocal. C has no closures, so week 7 builds them by hand: see closure conversion.
closure.e: let make () = let n = ref 0 in fun () -> incr n; !n
w: P.5 Recursion and functions as values

closure-conversion.d: Finding the names a block of code uses but doesn't define, so they can be passed in explicitly. In week 7 they become the fields of an outlined thread body's context struct: buffer pointers, values computed before the loop and enclosing loop counters.

cmplt.d: The .uir less-than comparison. It returns a bool, and any NaN makes it false.

coalescing.d: The GPU combining a warp's loads of neighboring addresses into a few wide transactions of 32 bytes each. When threads read addresses far apart, each costs a transaction of its own, mostly wasted.

commutative.d: An op whose operand order doesn't change the result, such as add and mul. Rewrites use this to put operands in canonical order.

compiler.d: A program that translates a program from one form to another, usually from something people write into something a machine runs.

compute-capability.d: The version of an NVIDIA GPU's architecture, written sm_XY in build flags: sm_75 for a T4, sm_89 for an RTX 40-series card. int8 tensor cores need sm_72 or newer. -arch=native builds for the GPU in the machine.

conservative-bounds.d: An interval that may be wider than the true range but never narrower. Too wide is always safe, because it just proves fewer things. Too narrow is a bug.

const.d: The .uir op for a fixed value. In text a constant is written as its literal, like 3, 0xff or true, and there's no const keyword.

constant-folding.d: Replacing an op whose inputs are all constants with its result, at compile time.

contiguous.d: Stored back to back in memory with no gaps. In a row-major tensor the last axis is contiguous: its stride is 1.

contraction.d: A compiler fusing a * b + c into one fused multiply-add, which rounds once instead of twice and so changes f32 bits. clang's -ffp-contract=off and nvcc's -fmad=false turn it off.

convolution.d: Sliding a small window of weights over an input and taking a weighted sum at each position. The workhorse of image models.

correlation.d: Sliding a window of weights over an input without flipping the weights. What machine learning calls a convolution, including every convolution in this course, is a correlation.

cross-entropy.d: The usual loss for classification, and the one lesson 6.5 trains MNIST with: -log of the probability the model gives the right label, averaged over the batch. It's small when the model puts high probability on the right answer.

dag.d: A directed acyclic graph: nodes with arrows and no cycles. A program as a DAG lets shared subexpressions be one node used twice.
dag.e: (a+b)*(a+b) has one a+b node with two users

dataclass.d: A Python class whose fields are declared once, with __init__ and friends generated for you. frozen=True makes it immutable, a good fit for IR nodes. It plays the role of an OCaml record.

detach.d: The .uir op that keeps a value but passes no gradient through it, so the value counts as a constant.
detach.e: gradient (mul x (detach x)) x is x, not 2x

dot-product.d: Two vectors of the same length multiplied element by element, then summed. Each element of a matmul is one dot product.

dtype.d: A value's element type. In .uir: void, bool and i32 in week 1, f32 from week 2 and i8 in week 9.

dune.d: OCaml's build tool. dune build compiles your project, and dune exec runs it. Python has no build step: you run your compiler with python main.py.

edge-values.d: The inputs the grader tries in every param slot to check a simplification: 16 hand-picked values per dtype, including INT_MIN, and from week 2 -0.0, infinity and NaN, plus 8 random ones, all inside each param's limits. With two params, every pair is tried. f32 results must match bit for bit.

effect.d: Something that changes memory instead of producing a value: a store, an mma (from week 9), or an end that repeats effects. Effects have dtype void.

elementwise.d: An op applied to each element separately, position by position.

emulator.d: The grader's way to run your CUDA without a GPU. It compiles the .cu file as C++, runs blocks one after another and runs each block's threads as real threads with a real barrier. It checks bits, but it can't measure speed.

end.d: The .uir op that repeats its effects once for every value of a range, then closes the range.

enum.d: A Python class whose members are a fixed set of named values, such as the ops of an IR. It plays the role of an OCaml variant whose constructors carry no data.

environment.d: A map from param slot to value for the call being evaluated. The usual way to implement substitution in an interpreter.

eviction.d: Throwing a line out of a cache to make room for another. Using that data again means fetching the line again.

exhaustiveness-check.d: OCaml's warning when a match misses a constructor of a variant. A catch-all _ case hides new constructors from it. Python's match has no such check.

exit-code.d: The number a program returns to whoever ran it, 0 for success. The grader doesn't read it for a test file, where your compiler prints an outcome line instead. render and render-cuda exit 2 for a program they refuse.

expand.d: The .uir op that broadcasts: a scalar becomes a vector, or size-1 axes grow to a target shape.

f32.d: A 32-bit floating-point number (IEEE binary32), in .uir from week 2. Every f32 op rounds its result to the nearest representable value.
f32.e: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 in f32, though not in doubles

false-sharing.d: Two threads writing different data in the same cache line. The line bounces between cores, which is slow even though there's no race.

fission.d: Splitting one loop into several, the opposite of fusion. Materializing a value fissions the work: one pass writes the temp buffer and later passes read it.

fixpoint.d: The state where applying the rewrite rules again changes nothing. A simplifier runs passes until it reaches one.

flash-attention.d: Attention computed without writing the table of scores, which grows with the square of the sequence length. Keys stream through shared memory, and each thread keeps an online softmax in registers. Same math as the three-kernel version, not the same bits.

flat-index.d: The single position of an element in a buffer, computed from a multi-dimensional index and the strides.

flop.d: One floating-point operation, such as an add or a multiply. Work divided by time gives FLOP/s, a measure of speed.

fold.d: Combining a list into one value step by step. A left fold combines from the first element onward. A reduce is a left fold. OCaml has List.fold_left, and Python has functools.reduce.

forward-mode.d: Autodiff that pushes one input's change forward through the program. It needs one pass per input, so training, with one loss and many weights, uses reverse mode.

fragment.d: A tile for a tensor-core instruction, spread across the registers of a warp's 32 threads. wmma fills one with load_matrix_sync and writes one back with store_matrix_sync.

fused-multiply-add-fma.d: One instruction computing a*b + c with a single rounding. It gives different f32 bits than two separate ops, which is why the grader compiles with -ffp-contract=off.

fusion.d: Computing a value where it's needed, every time it's needed, instead of storing it. Saves memory traffic, costs arithmetic.

gemm.d: General matrix multiply, C = A @ B. Most of the compute in a neural network.

grader.d: The course's test runner, tools/test.py. It compares your compiler's behavior to the oracle's on every test.

gradient.d: How fast a number changes when you wiggle each input. The .uir op gradient y x gives it with x's shape.

gradient-descent.d: Training by repeated small steps: compute the loss's gradient with respect to the weights, then move the weights a little against it. The MNIST test is 50 such steps.

graph.d: A set of nodes connected by arrows (edges). Unlike a tree, two arrows can point to the same node, so shared work is stored once instead of copied.
graph.e: (2 + 3) * (2 + 3) has one add node with two arrows out

grid.d: All the blocks of one kernel launch. They run in any order, many at once, and a block can never wait for another. In .uir a global loop is the grid.
grid.e: %b = range 3 axis=global is a grid of 3 blocks

hardware-prefetcher.d: A part of the CPU that spots loads at a regular stride and fetches the next cache lines before they're asked for. It can make a strided walk look less slow than a simple cache model predicts.

hash-consing.d: Building every node through a table, so two nodes with the same op, sources and arg are the same node. Equality becomes one pointer comparison.
hash-consing.e: two bindings of add 2 3 become one node

hash-table.d: A dictionary: give it a key and it quickly gives back the stored value. OCaml's is Hashtbl, and Python's is dict.

hex.d: Writing numbers in base 16, with digits 0-9 then a-f, marked with 0x.

hex-float.d: A float written in base 16 with an exponent, which C reads back exactly. Your renderer prints f32 constants this way.

hoisting.d: Moving a computation out of a loop because it doesn't change between iterations.

horner-s-rule.d: Evaluating a polynomial from the highest coefficient down, as c0 + x(c1 + x(c2 + ...)). One multiply and one add per term.

i32.d: A 32-bit signed integer in two's complement. add, mul and shl wrap around instead of failing.

i8.d: Week 9's 8-bit two's complement dtype, -128 to 127, for memory only: buffers, allocs and casts. There are no i8 literals or arithmetic: cast to i32 to compute. A cast to i8 keeps the low 8 bits.

identity.d: Whether two names point to the exact same object in memory (is in Python, == in OCaml), rather than two separate copies that happen to hold equal data.
identity.e: a is b is true only for the exact same node object

im2col.d: Image to columns: laying every window of the input out as one matrix, so a convolution becomes a matrix multiply. Writing that matrix to memory copies each input value once per window that covers it.

implementation-defined.d: Behavior the C standard lets each compiler choose, as long as it documents the choice. Different from undefined behavior.
implementation-defined.e: converting 3000000000 to int32_t: every compiler you'll use wraps

implicit-gemm.d: Running a convolution as a GEMM without writing out the im2col matrix: as the kernel copies a tile into shared memory, it works out where each element comes from in the image.

index.d: The .uir op that picks elements by position, dropping leading axes. Bounds must prove every index in range, or the program is rejected.

inline.d: Replacing a call with its body, params substituted. Always allowed for a pure call.

interpreter.d: A program that runs another program directly instead of translating it. Your week 1 compiler starts as one.

interval.d: A pair [lo, hi] meaning every value between them, used in bounds analysis.
interval.e: mod x 8 is in [0, 7], whatever x is

ir.d: Intermediate representation: the form a compiler holds a program in between reading it and printing output. The course's IR is a graph of UOps.

kernel.d: One function your compiler generates to do the work, here a C function named kernel that takes the buffers as pointers. From week 7 the word also means a loop nest that runs as one unit: the code between one materialization and the next. On a GPU (week 8) a kernel is a __global__ function that every thread runs, one per global loop.

kernel-form.d: What render-cuda accepts: every computation inside a global loop at the top level, and each kernel using only buffers, literals, its own ranges and its own shared memory. A program that isn't in kernel form is still a valid program, and render still prints C for it, but render-cuda exits 2.

l2-cache.d: The second level of cache. On a CPU it holds a few hundred KB to 2 MB per core. On a GPU one L2 is shared by every SM (32 MB on the 4060 Ti), so a tile one block loaded may still be there for the next.

lambda-calculus.d: Alonzo Church's language from the 1930s with only variables, function definitions and function application. It can express any computation, and its one evaluation step is beta reduction.

lane.d: One position in a group that works in step: one of the 4 or 8 values a SIMD instruction handles (week 7), or one of the 32 threads of a warp (week 9). Each SIMD lane is a separate output with its own rounding.

latency.d: How long one access takes from request to answer: about 100 ns for a CPU's main memory, hundreds of cycles for a GPU's global memory. A GPU hides it by running other warps while one waits.

learning-rate.d: How far one training step moves the weights along the gradient.

lexer.d: The part of a compiler that splits source text into words (tokens).

linearize.d: Turning a graph into an ordered list of steps, with loops nested where they belong. Both your interpreter and render work from this order.

literal.d: A fixed value written directly in source text, like 7, 3.5, or true. Inside the compiler, every literal becomes a CONST node with no sources.
literal.e: in %a = add 2 3, both 2 and 3 are literals

little-endian.d: A byte order where each number's lowest byte comes first. x86 and ARM use it.

load.d: The .uir op that reads memory through a view into a value.

load-placement.d: The rule for which loop a load runs in. Like any value it sits at the depth of its ranges, except that it moves into a loop holding all its uses when that loop writes the version it reads.

local-memory.d: CUDA's name for a thread's own memory that doesn't fit in registers. It lives in global memory, behind the caches, so it's slow. An array indexed by a value the compiler can't know at compile time ends up there. It has nothing to do with axis=local.

logit.d: A raw score a model gives one class, before softmax turns the scores into probabilities.

loop-carried.d: A value one iteration produces and the next iteration reads, like an accumulator.

loop-invariant.d: A value that's the same in every iteration of a loop, so it can be hoisted out.

lru.d: Least recently used: the policy that, when a cache is full, evicts the line that was used longest ago.

mantissa.d: The 23 bits of an f32 that hold its digits. The exponent field says where the binary point goes.

mask.d: A bool deciding whether a computed value is used or replaced, typically with where. Padding uses a mask to put zeros outside the data.

materialize.d: Computing a value once into a temporary buffer and reading the buffer wherever it's used. In .uir, stage forces it.

max-ops.d: A simplify test's op budget: the most ops your output may print, not counting literals, atom bindings like %y = %x, and params. Duplicate bindings each count, so hash cons what you print.
max-ops.e: max_ops=0 allows only literals and params

memoization.d: Remembering each node's result so shared work runs once. Without it, a graph with lots of sharing takes exponential time.

mixed-radix-rule.d: Week 8's rule that no two threads or blocks write the same element. Write the offset as a sum of digits, each a loop index (or its div or mod by a literal) times a literal. Sorted by coefficient, each must exceed the most all the smaller digits can add up to, like hours, minutes and seconds.

mma.d: Matrix multiply-accumulate, C = C + A·B on small tiles, the instruction a tensor core runs. In .uir, mma is an effect like store: it adds the product of two 16×16 i8 tiles into an i32 tile, wrapping like add.

movement-op.d: An op that rearranges elements without computing anything: reshape, permute, pad, shrink, expand.

mutant.d: A copy of the reference compiler with one plausible bug planted in it. The tests must make every mutant fail, which proves they catch that kind of mistake.

nan.d: Not a number: the f32 result of things like inf - inf or 0/0. Every ordered comparison with NaN (like cmplt) is false, but in .uir asserts NaN equals NaN.

ndim.d: The number of axes a tensor has, the same as its rank.

negative-zero-0-0.d: A second zero in f32 with its sign bit set. It compares equal to 0.0, but recip tells them apart (-inf vs inf).

newton-s-method.d: Improving a guess with a step that roughly squares the error. For a square root the step is (y + x/y) / 2. The spec's sqrt takes one step to fix its last few ulps.

numel.d: The total number of elements in a tensor: the product of its shape. A scalar has numel 1.

occupancy.d: How many warps an SM holds at once, which decides how well it can hide memory latency. It depends on each block's registers and shared memory: 65,536 registers at 64 per thread is 1,024 threads.

one-hot.d: A label written as a row with 1.0 at the true class and 0.0 everywhere else.

online-softmax.d: Softmax in one pass: keep a running max m, a running sum l and a running output, and when m goes up, rescale l and the output by exp(old m - new m). Lesson 9.5 calls it a running softmax, and flash attention is built on it.

opam.d: OCaml's package manager. It installs compilers and libraries such as dune. Python's counterpart is pip, though this course's Python track needs only the standard library.

open-range.d: A range a value depends on that no end has closed yet. A value with open ranges lives inside those loops.

operand.d: One of the input values passed to an operation. In add %a %b, both %a and %b are operands.

option.d: An OCaml type for a value that may be missing: Some v or None. Code that uses one has to handle both. Python uses None for a missing value, and a type hint such as int | None says it may be missing, but nothing forces you to check.
option.e: match o with Some v -> v | None -> 0

oracle.d: The reference compiler, _reference/uirc.py. Run it to see what any program should do. The grader compares you to it. Don't read its source.

outcome.d: What your compiler prints for each test file: MATCH, MISMATCH, REJECTED or OVERBUDGET, a space and the path. A test's file name says which one it expects.

outer-product.d: The matmul of a column and a row, with K = 1: every cell of the result is one multiply.

outlining.d: Moving a block of code into its own function. Week 7 outlines each thread loop's body so uir_parallel_for can call it once per iteration, with what it needs from outside in a context struct.

overflow.d: A result too big for its type. i32 overflow wraps in .uir, but in C, signed overflow is undefined behavior.

pad.d: The .uir movement op that grows a tensor with zeros on each side of each axis.
pad.e: pad [1 2] by 1 on both sides gives [0 1 2 0]

param.d: A function input in .uir: a param with slot=N is slot N of the enclosing call. Its first source is the shape, [] for a scalar, and an optional second source gives limits that every argument must fit.

parser.d: The part of a compiler that works out the structure of the words the lexer found.

pattern-match.d: OCaml's way of branching on the shape of a value, naming its parts as it goes. Python 3.10 has the same idea in its match statement, with class patterns such as case Add(x, y):.
pattern-match.e: match card with Number (n, _) -> n | Ace _ -> 11

per-thread-memory.d: Week 9's rule for an alloc of a kernel whose every load and store is in a local loop at t·S + e, with one S, 0 ≤ e, e + size ≤ S, and none an mma operand. No thread can see another's slice, so render-cuda may give each thread its own array, which sits in registers when every e is a literal.

permute.d: The .uir movement op that reorders axes. A transpose is permute [1 0].

phase.d: One of the consecutive local or warp loops inside a global loop. Every thread finishes one phase before any thread starts the next, so render-cuda puts a __syncthreads() after each, and a later phase may read anything an earlier one wrote.

physical-equality.d: Asking whether two values are the very same object in memory: one pointer comparison. OCaml writes it ==, Python writes is. With hash consing, equal expressions are the same node, so physical equality is all a rewrite needs.

pointer.d: A variable holding an address. *p reads what it points at, and p + 1 moves by one element, not one byte.

post-order.d: A depth-first order that lists each node after its operands. Autodiff visits it in reverse, so every node comes before the nodes it uses.

postfix-rpn.d: Writing each operator after its operands, also called reverse Polish notation. It needs no parentheses, and a stack evaluates it left to right.

private-alloc.d: In week 7, an alloc whose every load and store is inside one thread loop. Each iteration gets its own copy starting at zero, and the rendered C declares it inside the outlined function.

pure.d: Having no side effects: the same inputs always give the same result and nothing else changes. Pure calls can be inlined or computed once.

quantization.d: Storing a model's numbers in fewer bits, such as int8, so it needs less memory and can use faster units. int8 matrix multiplies on tensor cores are how many models are served after quantization.

race.d: Two threads touching the same memory at the same time, at least one of them writing, so the result depends on timing. The spec rules races out before running: the slice rule in week 7, the mixed-radix rule and phases in week 8.
race.e: two iterations both do o[0] = o[0] + 1: one increment is lost

range.d: The .uir loop counter: range n takes the values 0 to n-1. The name it is bound to is the loop's name.

rangeify.d: The pass that removes shapes from ops by asking each value for its element at an index, turning whole-tensor programs into loops.

rank.d: The number of axes a value has. A scalar is rank 0, a vector rank 1, a matrix rank 2.

recip.d: The .uir reciprocal, 1/x, on f32. recip 0.0 is inf and recip -0.0 is -inf.

reduce.d: The .uir op that collapses leading axes with add, mul or max, as a left fold from the first element.

ref.d: An OCaml mutable cell. ! reads it and := writes it. Python has no separate cell: variables and attributes can be reassigned directly.

register.d: One of a few dozen named storage slots inside the CPU, where arithmetic actually happens. On a GPU each thread has its own registers, up to 255 (about 1 KB), the fastest memory there is. A register has no address, so an array stays in registers only when every index is known at compile time.

register-spill.d: When code needs more values at once than there are registers, the compiler stores some to memory and loads them back, which is slow. A 16×16 upcast tile needs 32 AVX2 vector registers, and there are only 16.

render.d: Printing the program as C. From week 2 your compiler has a render command whose C the grader compiles and runs.

reshape.d: The .uir movement op that reads the same elements, in row-major order, under a new shape.

restrict.d: A C qualifier promising that a pointer's memory doesn't overlap any other pointer's. The compiler can then keep loaded values in registers across stores. .uir buffers never alias, so the promise holds. CUDA spells it __restrict__.

reverse-mode.d: Autodiff that walks backward from the loss. One walk gives the gradient with respect to every input at once.

rewrite-rule.d: A pattern and a replacement: wherever the pattern matches, put in the replacement.

ring.d: A number system whose add and multiply are associative and commutative, with multiply distributing over add. i32 with wraparound is a ring, so rules like regrouping a sum are valid for it. f32 isn't one, because rounding breaks associativity.
ring.e: (a + b) + c equals a + (b + c) for every i32

roofline.d: The bound on a kernel's speed: it can't run faster than its arithmetic alone or its memory traffic alone, so its time is at least the larger of the two.

round-to-nearest-even.d: The f32 rounding rule: go to the nearest representable value, and on an exact tie go to the one whose last bit is 0.

row-major.d: Storing a tensor so the last axis changes fastest: a matrix is stored row after row.

runtime.d: The part of the system that compiles the rendered C, runs it and reads the results back.

sanitizer.d: A compiler mode that adds run-time checks for undefined behavior. The grader builds your C with -fsanitize=undefined -fsanitize-trap=undefined (UBSan, the undefined behavior sanitizer), so signed overflow or a bad shift crashes the test instead of quietly working.

scalar.d: A single value with no axes: shape ().

schedule.d: The order a compiler runs operations in. Loads of a version have to be scheduled before the store that overwrites it. From week 7 it also means a program's plan for speed: how its loops are tiled and which axis each loop gets. A schedule changes the speed, never the bits.

sha-256.d: A hash that turns any file into a 64-hex-digit fingerprint. Change one byte and the fingerprint changes.

shape.d: The size of each axis of a value, written as a tuple. () is a scalar, and (3, 4) is a 3 by 4 matrix.

shared-memory.d: Fast memory on an SM shared by the threads of one block, tens of kilobytes per block. In .uir it's an alloc used only inside one global loop. Every block's copy starts at zero, so the rendered kernel clears it first.

shrink.d: A window. On memory it's a view into a buffer (week 2), and on a value it's a sub-tensor at given offsets (week 5).

simd.d: Single instruction, multiple data: one instruction that does the same operation on 4 or 8 adjacent values. Each lane is a separate output, so every result rounds exactly as before.

simplify.d: Your compiler's second command: rewrite %out to fewer ops while computing the same value for every input.

slice-rule.d: Week 7's rule against races. In a thread loop, every store, and every load of memory the loop also stores into, must be at offset r * S + e, with S a positive literal, e independent of r, 0 ≤ e and e + size ≤ S, and one S per buffer. Memory the loop only reads may be read anywhere.
slice-rule.e: iteration r owns elements r·S to r·S + S - 1

slot.d: A numbered position: a param's input number in a call, or a buffer's position in the kernel's arguments.

sm.d: Streaming multiprocessor: one of a GPU's processors. A block stays on one SM from start to finish, and the SM runs its threads 32 at a time, in warps. The RTX 4060 Ti has 34.

softmax.d: Turns scores into probabilities: e raised to each score, divided by the sum of all of them.

spec.d: The written rules of the .uir language for each week, in spec/uir-weekN.md.

src.d: The list of nodes a UOp takes as inputs (its sources).

stack.d: The .uir op that joins values of one shape along a new leading axis.

stage.d: The .uir op that tells the compiler to materialize a value into a temp buffer. Same value, different cost.

store.d: The .uir op that writes a value into memory through a view. It produces an effect, not a value.

stride.d: How far apart, in elements, two neighbors along an axis are in memory. In a row-major (3, 4) matrix, axis 0 has stride 4 and axis 1 stride 1.

structural-equality.d: Comparing two values by walking both and comparing everything inside, so its cost grows with the size of the values. OCaml writes it =, and a Python dataclass with the default eq=True generates it for ==. Compare physical equality.

subnormal.d: An f32 smaller than the smallest normal f32, stored with less precision. The smallest positive one is about 1.4e-45.

subgraph.d: A node together with every source node it reaches. In a hash-consed graph, a node's id stands for its entire subgraph, so comparing two subgraphs takes one check.
subgraph.e: the subgraph of %c = mul %a %b includes %c, %a, %b and their sources

substitution.d: Replacing each param in a body with the matching argument. The mental model for how call works.

sugar.d: An op, such as sub or fdiv, that is shorthand for a few core ops and means exactly its expansion. The parser can expand it.
sugar.e: sub a b means add a (mul b -1)

taylor-series.d: A function written as a polynomial around a point. The spec's sin reduces its input to [-π/2, π/2], then uses r - r³/3! + r⁵/5! - ... up to r^13.

tensor.d: An array with any number of axes: a number has 0, a vector 1, a matrix 2.

tensor-core.d: A unit on each SM that runs a small matrix multiply-accumulate (mma) as one warp instruction, thousands of multiply-adds at once. The 4060 Ti has four per SM. .uir uses them on i8 tiles, so the bits still match exactly.

tile-major.d: Storing a matrix tile after tile, each tile's elements together, instead of row after row. Week 9 stores int8 matrices this way so every 16×16 tile starts at a multiple of 256 bytes, which meets wmma's 32-byte alignment.

tiling.d: Splitting loops into blocks (tiles) small enough that the data they reuse stays close, in cache, registers or shared memory, while it's reused. It changes which outputs are worked on side by side, never the order of the adds inside a sum.

toposort.d: Putting a graph's nodes in an order where every node comes after its sources.

transpose.d: A matrix with rows and columns swapped: element [i][j] of the result is x[j][i]. In .uir it's permute %x [1 0]. As a view it's free, but reading it row by row jumps through memory.

trip-count.d: How many times a loop's body runs. For nested loops it's the product of their bounds.
trip-count.e: a GEMM's innermost body runs M*N*K times

truncation.d: Rounding toward zero. C's integer division truncates, so -7 / 2 is -3. The course's div floors instead, so div -7 2 is -4.

tuple.d: An ordered, fixed-size sequence of values that cannot be changed after it is created. Because a tuple never mutates, it can be used as a hash table key, and order matters: (a, b) is not (b, a).
tuple.e: src = (%a, %b) is a 2-element tuple of source UOps

two-s-complement.d: How signed integers are stored: the top bit is worth minus 2^31 instead of plus. All ones means -1.

ulp.d: A unit in the last place: the gap between an f32 and the next one. Two results one ulp apart differ in the last bit.

undefined-behavior-ub.d: Code the C standard gives no meaning to, such as signed overflow or INT_MIN / -1. The compiler may assume it never happens, and the grader's sanitizer turns it into a crash.

unflatten.d: Turning a flat index back into one index per axis, the reverse of computing a flat index. Along axis k it's (f div stride_k) mod size_k.

unroll.d: Writing a loop's body out once per iteration instead of looping. Unrolling a 4096-element vector breaks the C size limit (week 4), but unrolling a small upcast loop lets array elements live in registers (week 7).

uop.d: The course's graph node: an op name, a tuple of sources (src) and an argument (arg), plus its dtype and shape.

upcast.d: A loop axis, axis=upcast, that means the same as a plain loop but renders unrolled: the body is emitted once per iteration with the index as a literal, so an accumulator array becomes plain variables in registers. The bound must be a literal from 1 to 32.

valid-convolution.d: A convolution whose window never leaves the input, so n inputs and a kernel of k give n - k + 1 outputs.
valid-convolution.e: 6 inputs and a kernel of 3 give 4 outputs

variant.d: An OCaml type made of named alternatives (constructors), each possibly carrying data. In Python, an Enum covers alternatives with no data, and one dataclass per alternative covers the rest.

version.d: Memory as it is at one point in the program: the original buffer, or the buffer after some store. Each after makes a new version.

view.d: A window into memory made with shrink: a start offset and a length (or one element). Loads and stores go through views.

void.d: The dtype with no value. Asserts, stores, mmas, ends and the scalar shape marker [] are void.

warp.d: 32 threads of a block that an SM schedules together. A tensor-core instruction is issued by a whole warp. In week 9, axis=warp gives each warp one iteration, so a warp loop of 4 makes a block of 128 threads.

where.d: The .uir select: where c a b is a if c is true, else b. Both branches are evaluated.

wmma.d: CUDA's warp-level matrix API for tensor cores, in nvcuda::wmma: load_matrix_sync, mma_sync and store_matrix_sync on 16×16×16 tiles. render-cuda emits each mma as these calls, then __syncwarp().

wrap-around.d: Integer arithmetic that keeps only the low 32 bits, so going past the maximum comes back at the minimum.

zero-padding.d: Treating reads past the ends of the input as zeros, so a convolution gives as many outputs as inputs. Week 3 builds it with a clamp and a mask, week 5 with the pad op.
